entities.name: Geoffrey of Joinville
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Geoffrey de Joinville (c. 1226 – October 21, 1314), also known as Geoffroi de Geneville, was a prominent Anglo-French noble and Crusader whose career spanned the reigns of three English monarchs and deeply intertwined with the political landscape of 13th and early 14th-century England and Ireland. Hailing from the powerful House of Joinville in Champagne, France, his strategic marriage into the Lacy family established him as Lord of Trim in County Meath, Ireland, where he became a pivotal figure in the Anglo-Norman administration and expansion. His military prowess and diplomatic service rendered him a trusted confidant and loyal supporter of both Henry III and his son, Edward I, particularly during the Second Barons' War and the Edwardian conquests.

Born into a cadet branch of the illustrious Joinville family, Geoffrey was nephew to the renowned chronicler Jean de Joinville. His fortunes shifted significantly upon his marriage to Maud de Lacy, daughter and co-heir of Gilbert de Lacy, around 1252. This union brought him the Lordship of Trim and its substantial associated lands in the Lordship of Ireland, along with the title 1st Baron Geneville. He participated in the Seventh Crusade (1248–1254) alongside Louis IX of France and later served Henry III against Simon de Montfort during the Second Barons' War (1264–1267), enduring imprisonment after the Battle of Lewes. Under Edward I, he held significant offices, including Justiciar of Ireland from 1273 to 1276, where he actively pursued the expansion of English royal authority and the suppression of local Gaelic resistance. His later years involved further military service in Wales and Scotland, and he was summoned to Parliament as Baron Geneville from 1295 until 1307.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Geoffrey of Joinville's role as Justiciar of Ireland and Baron of Trim significantly consolidated Anglo-Norman power in Meath and strengthened English administrative structures in the 13th-century Lordship of Ireland, impacting regional governance for centuries. His career exemplifies the Anglo-French aristocratic network that shaped medieval British Isles.
